title: Beyond green iron: What China’s steel transition really means for Australia
gist: Australia's green iron thesis rests on an assumption that China will decarbonise steel via hydrogen-based DRI, but China's younger, larger blast-furnace fleet means it will instead combine efficiency upgrades, more scrap, gradual EAF growth, hydrogen demos and falling steel demand — so green iron demand emerges later and smaller than Canberra expects. China missed its 15% scrap-EAF target for 2025 (stuck near 10%) and crude steel output fell below one billion tonnes in 2025 for the first time since 2020, with lower output, not technology, the largest driver of emissions cuts.

insights.claim: China produces more than half of the world's steel, making its specific decarbonisation pathway — not just whether it decarbonises — the determinant of the global green iron trade.
insights.speaker: Xinyi Shen
insights.so_what: Any green iron project's demand curve is effectively a single-country bet; model China's route mix rather than global decarbonisation ambition.
insights.quote: China produces more than half (Opens in new window) of the world’s steel, making its decarbonisation pathway critical to the future of global green iron trade.
insights.locator: Australia has big ambitions for green iron

insights.claim: China is likely to hit steel decarbonisation targets by combining more efficient blast furnaces, greater scrap use, gradual EAF expansion, hydrogen demonstration projects and declining steel demand — not by replacing one production route with another.
insights.speaker: Xinyi Shen
insights.so_what: The 'many small levers' pathway spreads capital across efficiency retrofits, scrap collection and EAF equipment rather than concentrating it in hydrogen DRI — reprice suppliers accordingly.
insights.quote: China is likely (Opens in new window) to combine more efficient blast furnaces, greater scrap use, gradual expansion of electric arc furnaces (EAF), hydrogen demonstration projects, and declining steel demand
insights.locator: Rather than replacing one production route

insights.claim: China's steel industry is larger, younger and structurally different from Europe's or Japan's — it invested heavily in modern blast furnace capacity over the past two decades, so premature scrapping is unlikely and analogies to European decarbonisation mislead.
insights.speaker: Xinyi Shen
insights.so_what: Asset age is the hidden variable: young capital stock delays route-switching by a decade or more, pushing back the green iron demand ramp.
insights.quote: China’s steel industry is larger, younger, and structurally different from those of Europe or Japan.
insights.locator: Yet this assumption overlooks an important reality

insights.claim: For the coming decade, hydrogen DRI is more likely to complement than replace existing Chinese production routes, with commercial deployment constrained by the cost of green hydrogen and the need for new infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Xinyi Shen
insights.so_what: A ten-year horizon on hydrogen DRI at scale means green iron offtake contracts signed today face a long demand gap — check project financing assumptions.
insights.quote: For the coming decade, hydrogen DRI is more likely to complement than replace existing production routes.
insights.locator: Hydrogen-based steelmaking is likely to play a role

insights.claim: China's revised steel capacity replacement rules emphasise replacing outdated capacity and encouraging higher-quality, lower-emissions production including EAFs — signalling quality and efficiency improvement plus electrification and overcapacity management, not an immediate technological leap.
insights.speaker: Xinyi Shen
insights.so_what: Read Chinese steel policy as consolidation-and-efficiency, which supports scrap and EAF equipment demand while deferring hydrogen infrastructure.
insights.quote: the reforms suggest policymakers are focused on improving the quality and efficiency of the existing steel sector and accelerating electrification, while addressing persistent overcapacity
insights.locator: Recent policy developments reinforce this more gradual approach

insights.claim: China missed its target of producing 15% of steel through scrap-based EAFs by 2025, with the share remaining around 10%.
insights.speaker: Xinyi Shen
insights.so_what: A hard, verifiable miss against an official target — the cleanest benchmark for discounting future Chinese transition timelines.
insights.quote: China’s target of producing 15% of steel through scrap-based EAFs by 2025 was missed (Opens in new window), with the share remaining around 10%.
insights.locator: EAF expansion has also proved slower than expected

insights.claim: The barrier to Chinese EAF expansion is economics rather than technology — low profitability, weak demand, overcapacity and limited scrap availability continue to favour blast furnace production.
insights.speaker: Xinyi Shen
insights.so_what: EAF adoption is a margin story, so watch Chinese steel profitability and scrap availability as the real leading indicators, not policy announcements.
insights.quote: The barrier is not technological unavailability, but economics, as low profitability, weak demand, overcapacity and limited scrap availability continue to favour blast furnace production.
insights.locator: The barrier is not technological unavailability

themes.theme: Demand decline as the dominant driver

insights.claim: In 2025 China's crude steel production fell below one billion tonnes for the first time since 2020, and lower output — not technological change — was the largest driver of emissions reductions in the sector.
insights.speaker: Xinyi Shen
insights.so_what: Falling volume, not greener volume, is doing the decarbonisation work — bearish for total iron ore tonnage regardless of the green premium story.
insights.quote: In 2025, China’s crude steel production fell (Opens in new window) below one billion tonnes for the first time since 2020 and lower output, not technological change, was the largest driver of emissions reductions in the sector.
insights.locator: Demand itself will also shape the transition

insights.claim: As Chinese steel demand keeps declining with the maturing property sector, structural change becomes as important as new technologies in the sector's emissions trajectory.
insights.speaker: Xinyi Shen
insights.so_what: Ties the iron ore complex to Chinese property structurally rather than cyclically — a persistent volume headwind for Australian miners.
insights.quote: As demand continues to decline with China’s maturing property sector, structural change will become just as important as new technologies.

insights.claim: With faster EAF deployment combined with a phase-down of blast furnaces, Chinese steel sector emissions could fall to nearly 37% below their 2020 peak by 2035.
insights.speaker: Xinyi Shen
insights.so_what: A quantified upper-bound decarbonisation scenario to 2035 — useful as the bull case ceiling when sizing green iron demand.
insights.quote: the sector’s emissions could fall to nearly 37% (Opens in new window) below their 2020 peak by 2035
insights.locator: Combined, faster EAF deployment and a phase-down

insights.claim: Australian expectations about the timing and scale of Chinese green iron demand should be tempered — green iron will develop alongside more efficient blast furnaces, greater scrap use and expanding EAF production rather than displacing them.
insights.speaker: Xinyi Shen
insights.so_what: Directly challenges the demand assumptions underpinning Australian green iron project economics — stress-test offtake timing before committing capital.
insights.quote: Expectations about the timing and scale of Chinese demand should be tempered.
insights.locator: First, expectations about the timing and scale

insights.claim: Australia needs a diversified, adaptive green iron strategy prepared for multiple transition pathways rather than a single vision centred on China, with understanding China's evolving steel strategy as important as building domestic production.
insights.speaker: Xinyi Shen
insights.so_what: Single-buyer concentration risk is the core vulnerability in Australia's green iron plan; alternative markets are the hedge to look for in project plans.
insights.quote: Rather than betting on a single vision centred on China, Australia should prepare for multiple transition pathways.

insights.claim: Compatible standards, robust lifecycle carbon accounting and joint demonstration projects could reduce future green iron and steel trade barriers regardless of how quickly demand develops, making rule-setting a no-regrets Australian play.
insights.speaker: Xinyi Shen
insights.so_what: Standards and lifecycle carbon accounting are the option-value layer — watch for Australia-led certification schemes as an early indicator of trade architecture forming.
insights.quote: Compatible standards, robust lifecycle carbon accounting, and joint demonstration projects could reduce future trade barriers regardless of how quickly demand develops.
insights.locator: Third, Australia should help build the rules

insights.claim: The next phase of the Australia–China resources relationship will not be defined simply by exporting a greener version of the same commodity, breaking the assumed continuity from three decades of iron ore exports fuelling Chinese industrialisation.
insights.speaker: Xinyi Shen
insights.so_what: Undermines the simple 'green iron replaces iron ore' substitution narrative — the value migrates to standards, cooperation and supply chains, not just tonnes.
insights.quote: The next phase of that relationship will not be defined simply by exporting a greener version of the same commodity.
insights.locator: Australia’s iron ore exports helped fuel China’s industrialisation
